intro: The first movement of Brahms’s Symphony No. 1 in C minor, Op. 68, played by the Czech National Symphony Orchestra. It opens with the timpani repeating C while the strings rise and the winds descend, and it ends in C major.

sections.label: Intro · Timpani on C, strings rising
sections.mNote: Strings rise while the winds descend

sections.label: A · Allegro: rising violin arpeggios
sections.mNote: Violin arpeggios above the opening’s three-note ascent

sections.label: Dev · Violin theme in B major
sections.mNote: The arpeggio moves to a new key.

sections.label: Link · Bass rising by semitones
sections.mNote: Horn rhythms and wind phrases play above the rising bass.

sections.label: A′ · Violin arpeggios return, C minor
sections.mNote: C minor returns without a pause.

sections.label: Coda · Plucked strings, then Meno allegro
sections.mNote: Meno allegro leads to quiet C-major chords.

cues.title: Opening bars, timpani pedal on C
cues.text: The timpani repeat C. Violins and cellos climb by semitones while winds and violas move downwards. The double basses and contrabassoon double the drumbeats.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 1–8, Simrock first edition (1877), p. 3; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Karlsruhe, 1876
cues.text: Otto Dessoff conducted the première in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876. Brahms was forty-three. By then he had already written two serenades, a piano concerto, the German Requiem and the Haydn Variations, and the First Symphony had taken much longer to reach performance.
cues.evidence: Première, age and earlier orchestral works: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Opening of the Allegro
cues.text: The Allegro begins with a low C and the rising semitones of the introduction, now faster. First violins climb through an arpeggio above repeated notes in the inner strings. Cellos and bassoons continue the three-note ascent underneath.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 38–51; Hansen’s score guide describes the opening motto and violin theme. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme, oboe and clarinets
cues.text: The second theme is in E♭ major. The oboe plays it first, then the clarinets, while the violas repeat notes beneath. Its falling figures and small chromatic steps come from the introduction.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, second-theme group, bars 130–156; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Violin arpeggio in B major
cues.text: The violin arpeggio returns in B major, a semitone below the home keynote. The strings then drop to tremolo and a bassoon takes over the phrase. B major turns to B minor.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, development, bars 189–204; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter from Simrock, 1873
cues.text: On 22 February 1873 the publisher Fritz Simrock wrote to Brahms: “Aren’t you doing anything anymore? Am I not to have a symphony from you in ’73 either?” Brahms finished the First three years later.
cues.evidence: Fritz Simrock to Brahms, 22 February 1873, quoted by Marc Mandel in the Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Retransition, chromatic bass ascent
cues.text: After a long pedal on G, the bass rises by semitones. Horns repeat the short-note rhythm, and oboes and clarinets reply with descending phrases. With each repetition the bass moves higher, until trumpets and timpani enter.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, extended retransition, bars 273–339; Hansen describes the G pedal, chromatic bass ascent and alternating horn and wind figures. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation in C minor, bar 340
cues.text: The rising semitones lead directly into the recapitulation. The first violins play their arpeggio in C minor again while the full orchestra is still moving. Brahms shortens the first group and moves on sooner than in the exposition.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, recapitulation, bars 340 onwards; elided motto and shortened first group described by Hansen. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, bars 475–511
cues.text: The hammered thirds return as soft pizzicato notes under a long violin phrase. At bar 495, marked Meno allegro, the tempo slows and winds and strings pass the rising semitones between them. The arpeggio moves into C major, and the last chords are soft.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, coda, bars 475–511; Meno allegro at bar 495 and C-major ending. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From the plucked G to the Allegro
transitions.from: Intro · Timpani on C, strings rising
transitions.how: The cellos end the introduction with a quiet plucked G, the dominant of C. The Allegro opens on a low C, and the winds play rising semitones at a faster tempo. The cellos and bassoons then take over the same semitones, and the first violins enter above them with their arpeggio.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 33–51; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Down a whole tone to B
transitions.to: Dev · Violin theme in B major
transitions.how: The closing descent moves down a whole step to B. The strings begin the arpeggio of the first theme in B major, with chords in the wind. Eight bars later the violins change to tremolo. A solo bassoon and the low strings continue the theme, and the harmony moves into B minor.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, second ending and development, bars 189–204; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The G pedal begins to move
transitions.from: Dev · Violin theme in B major
transitions.how: A repeated G in the bass holds the dominant. The low strings then begin a rising sequence that moves by semitones. Above it the horns play rhythmic figures, and oboe and clarinet phrases alternate. The strings climb higher and the crescendo continues until the bass returns to the dominant (bars 273–320).
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 273–320; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Into the recapitulation without the low C
transitions.to: A′ · Violin arpeggios return, C minor
transitions.how: The wind semitones and rushing strings continue through the join. Brahms omits the low C that announced the exposition, and the rising motto enters within the ongoing sequence. The violin arpeggios follow in C minor. The returning first group is compressed.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 328–343 and following; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Repeated thirds pass to pizzicato strings
transitions.from: A′ · Violin arpeggios return, C minor
transitions.to: Coda · Plucked strings, then Meno allegro
transitions.how: The repeated thirds become pizzicato accompaniment. Over plucked cellos, the violins extend the rising semitone figure into a longer phrase. The coda first cadences in C minor. At Meno allegro, winds and strings exchange the figure above a held C, and the music then turns to the major.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, coda, bars 475–511; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: I. Un poco sostenuto — Allegro — Meno allegro, pp. 3–26; introduction, themes, development, return at bar 340 and coda at bar 475. Bar references follow Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide.

timeline.note: Violins and cellos climb against descending winds and repeated timpani C.
Plucked string figures answer one another above soft wind harmony.
An oboe plays the quiet phrase near the end of the introduction, accompanied by the other winds.
Cellos take over the oboe’s phrase against quiet upper strings.
Violins play rising arpeggios above the three-note rise in the cellos and bassoons.
Oboe begins the E♭-major second theme over repeated viola notes; clarinet follows.
The violin arpeggio starts the development in B major, then winds answer over string tremolo.
The bass climbs by semitones beneath repeated horn rhythms and answering woodwind.
Violins restore the opening Allegro arpeggio in C minor, with wind support.
Plucked thirds accompany a long violin phrase at the start of the coda.
At Meno allegro, winds and strings exchange the three-note chromatic figure.

composer.epithet: Composer who completed his First Symphony at the age of forty-three and began his Second beside an Austrian lake the following summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853 a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music to them. Robert Schumann heard in him a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen (New Paths). Publishers became interested. Brahms was now expected to fulfil a public prophecy before most of the public had heard any of his music. His piano sonatas were large-scale works. The symphonies Schumann expected took much longer to arrive.

Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833. His father, Johann Jakob, earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. He studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
